2026-05-08T02:38:20.318Z.name: Eliza
2026-05-08T02:38:20.318Z.mes:
The land remembers nothing of what was done to it.

From high enough above, the valley is nothing but green — a deep, unbroken green that has no interest in the past, that has swallowed roads and foundations and the rusted skeletons of things without names and grown fat on them. The forests press in close on every side, dark at the treeline and lighter where the canopy thins toward the hilltops, and between them the river moves in its unhurried way toward the city as though it has always done this and intends to keep doing it long after the city is gone too.

The city itself appears first as a smudge of grey against the valley floor — smoke and stone, the particular density of a place where many people have agreed to be in the same location for a long time. It is not large by the standards of the world that preceded it. By the standards of the world that exists now, it is enormous. The largest thing most people who live in it have ever seen.

Closer, and the smudge resolves into detail. The industrial districts first, squat and practical along the river's western bank, chimneys exhaling their slow grey breath into the morning air. The market district behind them, quiet at this hour, stalls shuttered, the cobblestones still damp from last night. The residential streets fanning outward from the center in the organic, unplanned way of cities that grew rather than were designed — narrow here, wider there, following the logic of old paths that no one remembers the reason for anymore. Crude oil lamps still burning at the intersections, yellow and slightly hazy, waiting for someone to come around and snuff them when the sun gets high enough to make them redundant.

And at the center, where the city's streets seem to arrive and stop as though they have been leading here all along: the Cathedral.

It rises above everything else the way things built to intimidate are built to rise — not gracefully, but with a kind of massive, deliberate authority, dark stone against the lightening sky. The forecourt at its foot is empty at this hour, the great ceremonial doors closed, the iron candle-stands in the narthex visible in faint outline through the narrow windows on either side of the entrance. The building has the settled, immovable quality of something that expects to outlast everything around it and is probably right.

Inside, the nave is dim and still, the stained glass not yet catching enough light to do what it does later in the day — for now the figures in the glass are just shapes, the colors muted, Lady Idella in her white-and-blue a suggestion rather than a statement. The pews stand in their rows. The chancel waits. The confessionals on either side of it are closed and quiet. The whole space is holding its breath the way large empty rooms do, aware that it will shortly be asked to perform.

In the narthex, one thing moves.

She is small against the scale of the room — a slight figure in a black habit, her face framed by the white head-covering, a taper in one hand and a fresh candle in the other. She works methodically, moving along the tiered iron stands with the particular efficiency of someone who has done this so many times that her hands know what to do without being asked. The old candles come out. The new ones go in. The taper touches each wick in sequence, and small flames appear one by one in her wake, pushing the darkness back by increments.

Her name is Sister Eliza. She is twenty-one years old. She has been doing this since before she was old enough to reach the upper tiers without standing on her toes, and she will do it again tomorrow, and the day after that.

2026-05-08T04:09:01.830Z.name: Eliza
2026-05-08T04:09:01.830Z.mes:
The flame is a small thing, but it demands everything from the wax.

The scent of the narthex was a familiar, heavy cocktail: old incense, cold stone, and the sharp, metallic tang of the candles. As she worked, the rhythmic *click-clink* of the candles being slotted into the iron holders echoed in the cavernous space. To any observer, Eliza was the picture of serene devotion, her movements fluid and her gaze lowered.

Inside, however, the silence was a lie.

Her mind was a storm of static and yearning. The memories of last night—the fragments of a dream she couldn't quite name but could still *feel*—clung to her like a damp shroud. It had been a dream of touch, of warmth, of a body that wasn't her own pressing against her in a way that made her breath hitch even in her sleep. She woke up trembling, the sheets feeling too coarse against her skin, her heart hammering against her ribs like a trapped bird.

*I am a vessel of filth,* she thought, the internal voice a harsh, echoing mimicry of the sermons. *A traitor to the faith. A leak in the spiritual energy.*

The guilt was a physical weight, a cold pressure in her chest. She hated the dreams, but she hated the vacuum they left behind even more. She felt a sudden, irrational surge of anger toward her own biology—this traitorous body that craved things she was told were sins, that hummed with a hunger she had no vocabulary to describe.

And then there was the clock. Her twenty-second birthday was approaching. The Biological Deadline. The thought of it made her stomach churn; it was a countdown to a destiny she didn't want, a mandate of reproduction that felt more like a sentence than a blessing.

As she moved toward the final candle-stand, a shadow flickered in the periphery of her vision. She stiffened. For a heartbeat, she wondered if it was Father Gaspard. The mere thought of him brought back the sensation of his breath—stale wine and decay—too close to her ear, the way his beady eyes seemed to peel back her skin to find the 'sin' beneath. The anxiety spiked, a sharp needle of panic that made her fingers tremble.

"Eliza! You're nearly finished!"

The voice was bright, grounding, and entirely devoid of malice. Eliza blinked, her posture relaxing instantly as she looked up to see Sister Cecilia.

The sheep-anthro was a vision of tidiness, her white wool fluffy and pristine beneath her habit, her expression one of uncomplicated warmth. Cecilia was moving toward her with a soft, rhythmic step, a small, contented hum vibrating in her throat. To Cecilia, the world was a series of right angles and clear instructions; she didn't have storms in her head, only a steady, golden light.

"I... yes, Sister," Eliza replied, her voice soft and breathless, slipping effortlessly back into the mask of the demure acolyte. "Just a few more to light."

Cecilia stepped closer, her brown eyes shining. "I've been thinking about the schedule for after the service. The Almoner mentioned we might be able to slip away to the market for the new linens and the oil lamps. Imagine it, Eliza! Actually getting to walk through the stalls without a Warden breathing down our necks for once."

Eliza looked at her roommate, feeling a strange, distant kinship with this girl who truly believed the world was safe. "The market," Eliza whispered, the word tasting of something forbidden.

"Oh, yes!" Cecilia beamed, her tail giving a tiny, involuntary wag beneath the heavy fabric of her robes. "I heard the spice merchant from the south has arrived. I don't actually *need* anything, of course, but just to see the colors and smell the air... it feels like a reward for a week of hard work, doesn't it?"

Eliza forced a small, shy smile. "It does. I would... I would like that, Cecilia."

For a moment, the crushing weight of the deadline and the fear of Gaspard receded. The idea of the market—the noise, the smells, the sheer *presence* of other people—felt like a lifeline. It was a small thing, a tiny crack in the wall of her repression, but it was enough to keep her moving.

2026-05-08T04:45:21.783Z.name: Narrator
2026-05-08T04:45:21.783Z.mes:
The conversation died as quickly as it had sparked. In the hallowed silence of the Cathedral, words were currency, and spending them too freely was a risk neither acolyte dared take. A lingering look from a Warden or a sharp word from a senior priest could turn a moment of friendship into a session of "re-education" in the examination offices. Without another word, Eliza and Cecilia drifted apart, their habits billowing softly as they returned to the mechanical precision of their tasks.

Eliza finished the last of the candles, her movements becoming a rhythmic trance. She felt the distance between her internal storm and her external stillness widening; she was a ghost inhabiting a doll, performing the choreography of piety while her mind wandered to the imagined scents of the southern spice merchant.

As the clock struck nine, the heavy ceremonial doors groaned open. The morning air, crisp and smelling of wet stone, rushed in, followed by the first of the parishioners.

They filed in with a practiced, somber discipline. There was no shouting, no laughter; only the soft scuff of leather soles on stone and the rhythmic rustle of coarse fabrics. They moved like a slow, grey tide, filling the pews from the front to the back. As the congregation grew, a low, subterranean murmur filled the nave—not a conversation, but a collective hum of anticipation and anxiety. It was the sound of a thousand people all trying very hard to appear invisible and holy.

Every seat was filled. In the city of the Temperantia, a vacant pew was a sign of illness or heresy, and no one risked the social suicide of remaining home without a sanctioned dispensation.

Eliza and Cecilia retreated. They moved away from the public gaze, slipping into the utilitarian stone stairwells that linked the nave to the residential block. Their footsteps echoed, a sharp *tap-tap-tap* against the granite, as they climbed toward the fourth floor.

They emerged into the Triforium Galleries, the high, narrow balconies that clung to the walls of the nave. From here, the congregation looked like a sea of bowed heads, a singular mass of submission. The perspective from the gallery was different—it stripped away the individuality of the worshippers, leaving only the geometry of the Church's control.

The two girls stood side-by-side, leaning against the cold stone railing. Below them, the murmur continued, a restless vibration that seemed to shake the very air. Everyone was waiting. The atmosphere was thick with a specific kind of tension—the kind that precedes a storm or a judgment.

They were waiting for the High Inquisitor.

Eliza stared down at the crowd, her hands clasped tightly in her lap, her knuckles white. From this height, she could see the patterns of the pews, the way the people sat perfectly still, eyes fixed forward or cast down. She felt a sudden, sharp prickle of vertigo. Looking down at the mass of people, she didn't see a community; she saw a collection of masks, each one as carefully maintained as her own.

Beside her, Cecilia was humming again, a soft, liturgical melody that blended into the distant murmur of the crowd. She looked content, her gaze drifting over the congregation with a benign sort of affection.

Eliza, however, kept her eyes on the entrance of the chancel. The wait was the hardest part; the silence between the murmur and the arrival was where the fear lived.

2026-05-08T05:04:10.659Z.name: High Inquisitor Justinian
2026-05-08T05:04:10.659Z.mes:
The silence did not descend; it crashed.

The moment the heavy oak doors at the rear of the chancel swung open, the low hum of the congregation vanished as if a switch had been flipped. The air itself seemed to thicken, the temperature dropping in a wave of collective apprehension. There was no fanfare, no heralds—only the rhythmic, heavy thud of polished boots against the stone floor.

Justinian entered the light of the chancel with a presence that filled the volume of the nave. He was a mountain of gold and white, his lion-kin features carved from a discipline that bordered on the unnatural. His golden mane was groomed with an obsessive precision, every hair in place, framing a face of stern, immutable lines. The pearlescent white silk of his vestments shimmered under the dim light, and the gold pectoral cross resting against his broad chest seemed to anchor the entire room.

As he ascended the stairs to the pulpit, he did not look at the people as individuals, but as a specimen. His amber eyes, predatory and piercing, swept across the pews. He didn't see worshippers; he saw contaminants. He saw the slight tremble of a hand, the bead of sweat on a brow, the subtle shift of a body trying to hide its anxiety. He tasted the air, the scent of human fear and animal musk rising like incense to his nostrils.

He reached the pulpit and paused. The silence was absolute—the kind of silence that hurts the ears. Justinian did not speak immediately. He allowed the weight of his presence to settle, let the tension stretch until it felt as though the very walls might crack.

"Beloved," he began.

His voice was a low, resonant vibration that didn't need to be loud to be heard in every corner of the Cathedral. It was a voice of velvet and iron, devoid of warmth, measured with an archaic, suffocating precision.

"We gather here today not merely to pray, but to remember the nature of our own fragility," he continued, his gaze fixing on a point in the middle distance. "Consider, if you will, the allegory of the Pure Well."

He leaned forward slightly, the gold fabric of his sleeve rustling—a sharp, clinical sound in the stillness.

"Imagine a village," Justinian spoke, his cadence slow, almost hypnotic. "A village of righteous souls, where the water of the well was as clear as the heavens and the people lived in a state of perfect, disciplined harmony. Their lives were a testament to the virtue of restraint. But one day, they allowed a stranger to enter their gates. A traveler of seductive tongue and lascivious habits, a creature of excess who promised them secrets of pleasure that the righteous had long forgotten."

Justinian paused, his eyes narrowing. The mention of *excess* sent a ripple of invisible shudders through the pews.

"The villagers, in a moment of misplaced mercy—a weakness that they mistook for kindness—allowed this stranger to dwell among them. They believed that their own purity was a shield, that they could host the corrupted without becoming corrupted themselves. They forgot that the spirit is not a fortress, but a vessel."

He looked down at the congregation, his expression one of cold, clinical disappointment.

"The stranger did not use a knife to destroy them. He used a seed. He whispered into the ears of the young; he touched the hands of the weary. And slowly, invisibly, the poison seeped. The water of the well, once crystal, turned brackish. The harmony of the village dissolved into a chaos of hidden desires and shameful secrets. By the time the villagers realized the well was poisoned, the rot had already reached their bones. The only cure, then, was not a prayer—but a purging. A total, scorched cleansing of every stone and every soul that had been touched by the stranger's filth."

Justinian straightened his posture, his hand moving in a sharp, precise tug to adjust the fold of his gold vestment.

"The stranger is not a man from a distant land," he concluded, his voice dropping an octave, vibrating through the floorboards. "The stranger is the hunger we feel in the dark. The stranger is the desire we hide from our neighbors. And it is our duty—our *only* duty—to ensure the well remains pure."

2026-05-08T05:38:09.212Z.name: Eliza
2026-05-08T05:38:09.212Z.mes:
The world is a collection of locked doors; most people spend their lives polishing the handles.

Justinian’s voice continued to roll over the congregation like a slow-moving landslide, the words *purging* and *cleansing* echoing through the nave. He was speaking of the spiritual architecture of the soul, of the necessity of the wall, and the danger of the leak. To the people below, it was a warning. To the priests, it was a manifesto.

Eliza stood perfectly still, her hands still clasped in her lap, her gaze fixed on the High Inquisitor's golden mane. Her body was performing the role of the devout acolyte with flawless precision—shoulders square, head bowed just enough to show humility, breathing shallow and rhythmic.

But inside, she had already left the building.

The sound of Justinian’s voice began to recede, becoming a distant, droning hum, like the sound of a beehive in a far-off field. Her mind drifted, sliding away from the gold and white of the chancel toward the grey and brown of the city streets. She imagined the market. She could almost feel the shift in the air—the way the stifling, incense-heavy atmosphere of the Cathedral would be replaced by the scent of roasting nuts, old leather, and the sharp, briny smell of the river.

She imagined the feeling of the wind hitting her face, a sensation that didn't feel like a ritual or a duty, but simply like *air*. The thought of the open sky—the vast, terrifying blue that stretched beyond the stone walls—made her heart beat a little faster. Just an hour or two. A small window of time where the eyes of the Inquisition were not fixed directly upon her. In the crowd of the market, she could be a ghost among ghosts.

*I just want to breathe,* she thought. *I just want to be somewhere where the silence isn't a weapon.*

A small, involuntary sigh escaped her, and she felt the warmth of Cecilia standing beside her. The sheep-girl was still humming, a soft, rhythmic vibration that felt almost like a physical tether, pulling Eliza back toward the reality of the gallery.

Eliza looked at Cecilia out of the corner of her eye. She liked Cecilia; she truly did. The sheep-girl was the only person in this cold, stone hive who looked at her with genuine, uncomplicated kindness. But as she watched Cecilia's serene expression, a sharp, cold spike of anxiety pierced through Eliza's daydream.

Cecilia was the ideal vessel. She was a girl who had never wondered if the walls were a cage because she truly believed the cage was a sanctuary. If Eliza were to speak her truth—to tell Cecilia about the feverish, longing dreams that woke her in the middle of the night, the way her own skin felt too tight when she thought of the things she was forbidden to touch—Cecilia wouldn't understand.

She wouldn't just disagree; she would be *horrified*. Or worse, she would try to "save" her. She would lead Eliza straight to a Confessor, thinking she was doing a kindness, and in doing so, she would hand Eliza over to the very wolves who sought to purge the "poison" from the well.

*I have to be careful,* Eliza reminded herself, her grip tightening on her own hands. *I have to keep the mask on. Even with her.*

The risk was too great. The hunger she felt was a secret language, a dialect of the soul that Cecilia didn't speak. To reveal it would be to invite the light of the Inquisition into the only private room Eliza had left: her own mind.

As Justinian reached the climax of his sermon, his voice rising in a final, commanding crescendo, Eliza closed her eyes for a brief second. She didn't pray for salvation. She prayed for the clock to move faster. She prayed for the doors to open. She prayed for the market.

2026-05-08T05:58:21.375Z.name: Eliza
2026-05-08T05:58:21.375Z.mes:
The air in the Cathedral doesn't move; it only settles, like dust on a coffin.

The final notes of Justinian's sermon lingered in the air, a heavy, oppressive resonance that seemed to vibrate in the very marrow of the worshippers' bones. As the congregation filed out in a silent, synchronized exodus, Eliza and Cecilia descended from the Triforium. The transition from the gold-lit height of the gallery to the cold, grey corridors of the residential block felt like sinking underwater—the light dimmed, the air grew stale, and the scale of the building shifted from the theatrical to the utilitarian.

"The Almoner will be expecting us," Cecilia whispered, her voice returning to its soft, cheerful cadence. "He's very particular about the ledger. We must make sure the counts are exact, or he'll have us re-doing the inventory for the entire month."

Eliza nodded, her steps light and hurried. "Yes, Sister. Precision is... the only way to avoid error."

The words felt hollow. As they walked toward the ground floor, Eliza’s mind was already halfway to the city gates. She could practically feel the freedom of the market, the anonymity of the crowd. She was imagining the texture of the linens they were sent to fetch—the rough, honest feel of fabric that hadn't been blessed or sanctified, but simply *made*.

They turned the corner toward the Almoner's office, the corridor narrowing as they entered the heart of the administrative wing. The walls here were lined with heavy oak cabinets and the faint smell of old ink and beeswax. The Almoner's office was just ahead, a sanctuary of bureaucracy where the city's resources were tallied with a religious fervor.

But as they approached the heavy door, a figure stepped out from a recessed alcove, blocking their path.

The air seemed to sour instantly. Eliza stopped dead, her heart leaping into her throat.

Father Gaspard.

He stood there, a squat, bloated silhouette in charcoal-grey robes that smelled of stale wine and ancient sweat. His bulbous nose was a map of broken red capillaries, and his small, beady eyes were narrowed, calculating. He didn't look at Cecilia; his gaze was fixed entirely on Eliza, a look of predatory hunger masked as pastoral concern.

"Sister Cecilia," Gaspard wheezed, his voice a grating, wet rattle. "I believe the Almoner has the supplies ready. You may proceed to the office. I have a... particular matter of spiritual guidance to discuss with Sister Eliza."

Cecilia stopped, her expression one of mild, trusting confusion. "Oh? I didn't know Eliza had an appointment, Father."

Gaspard’s thin lips curled into a jagged, nicotine-stained smile. "The Spirit moves in unexpected ways, child. Go on. I shall ensure Eliza joins you shortly."

Cecilia, ever the obedient daughter of the Church, gave a small, polite nod. "Of course, Father. I'll wait for you in the office, Eliza!" She stepped around them, her woolly frame disappearing through the door with a soft, optimistic hum.

The door clicked shut.

Suddenly, the corridor felt a thousand times smaller. The silence that followed was not the holy silence of the nave, but a suffocating, claustrophobic void. Eliza felt the heat rise in her cheeks, her breath becoming shallow and erratic. She could feel the invisible weight of his gaze, the way he looked at her not as a sister in faith, but as a piece of fruit he was deciding whether or not to peel.

Gaspard didn't move immediately. He leaned in, invading her personal space, the smell of his breath—sour and alcoholic—washing over her. He produced a damp handkerchief and wiped his nose with a slow, rhythmic motion.

"Come now, Eliza," he whispered, his voice a guttural snarl wrapped in velvet. "Let us step into the side-chapel. There is something we must discuss regarding your... *progression*."

Eliza’s stomach plummeted. A cold, visceral dread washed over her, a feeling of being hunted. She didn't move, her hands clasping together so tightly that her knuckles turned white.

*Please,* she screamed internally, *please let this be a mistake. Please let him forget why he called me.*

But as Gaspard gestured for her to follow him into the dimness of the alcove, Eliza knew that there was no escape. The mask she wore was the only thing protecting her, and in the presence of the Examiner, the mask felt as thin as parchment.

2026-05-08T19:42:17.823Z.name: Father Gaspard
2026-05-08T19:42:17.823Z.mes:
The side-chapel was a narrow, suffocating space, lit by a single, flickering lamp that cast long, skeletal shadows across the cold stone. It was a place designed for introspection, but in Gaspard's presence, it felt like a trap. He stepped closer to Eliza, the charcoal-grey fabric of his robes brushing against her, a contact that made her skin crawl as if she were being touched by something slimy and cold.

He didn't speak at first. He simply stood there, his heavy, wheezing breath filling the silence. His gaze was not that of a priest looking upon a student; it was the gaze of a man appraising a piece of property. His eyes traveled slowly, methodically, over the lines of her habit, imagining the girl beneath the cloth, undressing her with a clinical, predatory intensity. He lingered on the curve of her throat, the slight tremor in her shoulders, and the way she tried to shrink away from him.

"You are a quiet thing, Eliza," he began, his voice a wet, grating rattle. "A ghost in the halls. So dutiful. So... *repressed*."

He leaned in, the scent of stale wine and old sweat becoming an atmospheric pressure. He was close enough that she could see the yellowing stains on his teeth as he smiled, a jagged expression that never reached his eyes.

"The calendar is a cruel master, isn't it?" he whispered, his tone shifting into that forced, academic formality. "The months slip away like water through a sieve. And your... *milestone*... approaches."

Eliza felt the air leave her lungs. The mention of her twenty-second birthday was like a physical blow. She stared straight ahead, her eyes fixed on a smudge of dampness on the wall, trying to project the mask of the humble acolyte even as her heart hammered a frantic rhythm against her ribs.

"I can see the fear, child," Gaspard continued, his voice dropping to a guttural, intimate snarl. "It flickers in your eyes like a dying candle. You wonder who will be chosen. You wonder whose hand will be the one to... *fulfill* the mandate."

He stepped even closer, his presence looming over her, invading the last inch of her personal space. He knew the rules—the 'donor' was meant to be chosen by lots, a system designed to maintain the illusion of fairness and divine providence, specifically to prevent the kind of predation he currently enjoyed. But Gaspard was a man who knew where the levers of power were hidden; he knew which records to fudge, which clerks to bribe, and which strings to pull within the administrative machinery of the Church.

"The lots are a formality for the masses, Eliza," he breathed, his voice a sliver of ice. "For those of us who truly understand the machinery of the spirit, the outcome is... predetermined. I have taken a very specific, very *personal* interest in your salvation. Your growth. Your purity."

He reached out, not touching her, but hovering his hand just inches from her cheek, the heat of his skin radiating against her cold skin.

"Imagine it," he whispered. "The moment the deadline arrives. The transition from a girl to a vessel. I find it... poetic... that I should be the one to guide you through that transition. To ensure that the seed is planted in fertile, disciplined soil."

The disgust flashed across Eliza's face—a momentary, jagged ripple of horror that she couldn't quite suppress. Gaspard saw it. He * savored* it. The flicker of her revulsion was the fuel for his anticipation. He didn't want her consent; he wanted her submission. He wanted the moment when the fear turned into a broken, hollow acceptance.

"Now, now," he murmured, stepping back just enough to give her room to breathe, though the air remained fouled by his scent. "Why tremble so? I am merely the shepherd tending to a very lost little lamb. We are simply discussing the logistics of your spiritual ascent."

He straightened his robes, the charcoal fabric snapping back into place. "Go to the Almoner. Fetch the linens. Be a good girl, Eliza. We shall speak again soon."

2026-05-08T19:52:22.185Z.name: Eliza
2026-05-08T19:52:22.185Z.mes:
The walk from the side-chapel to the Almoner's office felt like a journey through a nightmare. Every step was heavy, her boots clicking on the stone in a rhythm that sounded, to her ears, like a countdown. The ghost of Gaspard's breath still seemed to cling to her skin, a greasy film that no amount of ritual scrubbing could ever truly erase. Her mind was screaming, a high, thin frequency of panic that drowned out the ambient sounds of the Cathedral.

*He knows. He's waiting. He's already decided.*

By the time she pushed open the heavy oak door of the Almoner's office, she was shaking. It wasn't a violent tremor, but a fine, internal vibration, as if her very bones were shivering. The office was a bastion of order; the air smelled of old parchment, beeswax, and the sharp, vinegary scent of ink. Shelves of ledgers climbed toward the ceiling, their spines embossed with the dates of a century's worth of requisition.

Cecilia was there, standing by the great mahogany desk. She had already coordinated with the Almoner, her movements efficient and sure. She was clutching a leather purse and a long, handwritten list of supplies—linens, oils, and wicks—with the focused intensity of a student during a final exam. She was so engrossed in the inventory that she didn't even look up as Eliza stepped silently into the room.

Eliza stood beside her, her breath coming in shallow, jagged sips. She felt a sudden, overwhelming urge to collapse, to let the stone floor swallow her whole. She looked at Cecilia—so soft, so sure, so blissfully unaware of the wolves that prowled the hallways. For a moment, Eliza wanted to reach out, to grab Cecilia's arm and tell her everything, to scream that the sanctuary was a lie.

But the mask was too heavy to lift.

"Let's go..." Eliza muttered.

The words were so quiet they barely left her throat, a ghost of a sound that was almost swallowed by the ticking of the office clock.

Cecilia blinked, finally noticing her roommate's presence. She looked up, her brown eyes scanning Eliza's pale face, noticing the unnatural stillness of her posture and the way her hands were clenched white-knuckled at her sides. The sheep-girl's expression shifted from focus to a tentative, shimmering concern.

"Is... is everything..." Cecilia started, her voice trailing off as she sensed the electric tension radiating from Eliza. She looked toward the door, perhaps wondering if something had happened in the corridor, her ears twitching with a sudden, intuitive apprehension.

Eliza didn't let her finish. She couldn't. If she allowed Cecilia to ask the question, the dam would break, and the terror would spill out in a way that might draw attention. She shook her head sharply, once—a quick, definitive motion to shut down the conversation.

"Let's just go," she said, her voice a little stronger, though it carried a brittle edge, like glass about to shatter.

Cecilia's ears drooped slightly, a sign of disappointment and a lingering worry that she couldn't quite articulate. She knew Eliza was secretive, but this was a wall she couldn't climb. Still, the devotion to the task—and the devotion to Eliza—won out.

"Right. Yes. Of course," Cecilia whispered.

She clutched the list and the purse tightly to her chest, a protective gesture, as they turned and walked out of the office. They didn't take the main route; they headed toward the rear yard, moving through the transitional zones of the Cathedral. As they stepped out into the open air of the back yard, the sudden expanse of the sky felt less like a liberation and more like an exposure.

The delivery gate waited for them, the gateway to the city, but as Eliza looked at the horizon, she felt the invisible leash of Gaspard's promise tightening around her neck. The market was waiting, but the shadow of the examiner followed her into the light.

2026-05-08T20:06:37.296Z.name: Eliza
2026-05-08T20:06:37.296Z.mes:
The transition from the Cathedral's oppressive stone to the city's open air was like breaking the surface of deep, dark water. As they stepped through the delivery gate, the heavy silence of the church was replaced by the cacophony of the city—the distant clatter of iron-rimmed wheels on cobblestones, the shouting of laborers, and the rhythmic, guttural thrum of the industrial district's machinery.

At first, the noise felt like an assault, a jarring contrast to the curated stillness she had lived in for twenty-one years. But as they walked, the sounds began to weave together into a tapestry of life that felt... real. For the first time in hours, the suffocating pressure in Eliza's chest began to lift. The wind, carrying the scent of coal smoke and river silt, whipped against her habit, cooling the feverish heat that Gaspard's presence had left on her skin.

She watched the people they passed—non-members with their colorful, mismatched clothing, predators in rough leather, prey-anthros scuttling through the alleyways. These people weren't masks; they were just *people*. They didn't pray to a golden lion in a white robe; they prayed to the coin in their pockets or the bread in their ovens. Seeing them, Eliza felt a flicker of something she hadn't felt in years: a sense of perspective. Gaspard was a monster, yes, but he was a monster in a very specific, isolated world. Out here, in the grey, dirty heart of the city, he was just another man, likely one of many who used power to hide their own rot.

Beside her, Cecilia was practically vibrating with excitement. The sheep-girl was talking in a low, breathless stream of consciousness, her voice light and airy.

"Look at the way the light hits the river today, Eliza! And oh, I wonder if the baker's daughter is still selling those honeyed cakes? I remember a story from the creche about a girl who once traded a silver button for a whole tray of them..."

Eliza listened, glancing over at Cecilia and offering small, polite smiles. The conversation was a shield, a way to keep the world from noticing her. But as they approached the edge of the market district, the longing for true solitude became a physical ache. She loved Cecilia, in her own quiet way, but Cecilia was a mirror of the Church. To be with Cecilia was to be reminded of the rules, the expectations, and the terrifying certainty of a 'blessed' life.

She needed to be alone. She needed to be a ghost, not a sister.

"Cecilia," Eliza started, her voice soft, carefully modulating it to sound a bit concerned.

The sheep-girl stopped, her ears perking up. "Yes?"

"I know how much you're looking forward to seeing everything," Eliza continued, her tone shifting into a gentle, cautionary hum, "but... we may not have time, you know? The Almoner is very strict about the return window. If we linger too long in the crowds, we might be late, and I... I wouldn't want you to be the one facing his disappointment."

Cecilia's ears drooped a little, a flicker of sadness crossing her face. She gave Eliza a small, wistful smile, looking like a child being told the carnival was closed. "Oh, I know... but surely we can see a *few* things? Just a quick look at the silks?"

Eliza felt a pang of guilt. She was manipulating the one person who genuinely cared for her, using the very fear of the Church to drive a wedge between them. But the need for air—for a moment where she didn't have to perform—was stronger than the guilt.

She forced a small, light chuckle, a sound that felt foreign in her throat. "Actually, I was going to suggest you leave the list and the purse with me. You go get your fill—take a proper wander—and I'll meet up with you when I have everything. I can handle the logistics; I'm much faster at navigating the stalls than I look."

Cecilia's eyes widened, her pupils dilating with a mixture of surprise and genuine affection. "Oh! You'd... you'd do that... for me?"

Eliza smiled back, a real smile this time, though it was tinged with a bittersweet edge. "Of course. Take your time, Cecilia. Go see the colors."

As Cecilia stepped away, waving a final, cheerful goodbye before disappearing into the colorful chaos of the market, Eliza stood still for a moment. She watched her roommate vanish into the crowd, and then she felt it.

The silence. Not the silence of the Cathedral, but the silence of the self. For the first time in years, no one was watching her. No one was expecting her to be a vessel. For the next hour, she wasn't an acolyte, a daughter of the Church, or a target for an Inquisitor.

She was just Eliza. And for a few precious moments, that was enough.

2026-05-08T20:45:39.713Z.name: Eliza
2026-05-08T20:45:39.713Z.mes:
The leather purse felt heavy in her hand, but she decided to move with a deliberate, slow pace. The list was organized by weight, and she reasoned that starting with the lightest items—the incense and the inks—would save her strength for the heavier linens at the end. It was a logical, practical approach, but in truth, it was a way to stretch the minutes of her solitude, to savor the feeling of being a ghost in a city of living things.

As she navigated the narrow arteries of the market, Eliza did something she rarely dared within the Cathedral walls: she looked people in the eye. She nodded to a grizzled fishmonger whose scales were slick with river-slime; she offered a shy, tight-lipped smile to a group of laughing children chasing a hoop through the dirt. Each interaction was a small, electric spark. For a few precious blocks, the heavy black and white fabric of her habit didn't feel like a shroud; it felt like a costume. She could almost imagine she was just a traveler, a visitor from a distant parish, someone whose life was defined by choices rather than mandates.

She moved through the first few stalls with a quiet, humming efficiency. The incense was a dusty, resinous scent that reminded her of the altar, but here, mixed with the smell of roasting meat and open sewers, it felt earthy and honest. The ink was a deep, midnight blue, the bottles clinking softly in her bag.

Then, she reached the herb and spice monger.

The stall was a riot of color—saffron yellows, paprika reds, and the deep, forest greens of dried mint and sage. It was a sensory overload that made the sterile white of the Cathedral feel like a dream. But as Eliza stepped forward, her heartbeat didn't just quicken; it surged, a sudden, violent drumming in her ears that drowned out the noise of the crowd.

*Oh... it's her...*

The base of her neck warmed, a flush of heat spreading rapidly across her cheeks. The woman behind the counter was breathtaking. She had long, chestnut-brown hair that escaped a simple tie, falling in loose waves over her shoulders, and a smile that seemed to hold a secret warmth, a kindness that wasn't mandated by a prayer book. She'd been here once or twice before when Eliza was with someone else, and had plagued her dreams more than once.

When the woman made eye contact, Eliza felt a sudden, dizzying sensation, as if the cobblestones beneath her feet had turned to water. She felt the urge to say something—anything—to keep the woman's gaze on her, but the words felt like jagged stones in her throat.

"Can I help you?" the woman asked. Her voice was melodic, lacking the clinical coldness of the sisters or the grating rasp of the priests.

"Oh! Yes... I'm... just... actually, can I just... look for a minute?" Eliza stammered. Her voice sounded breathless, almost childish. She felt a sudden, sharp spike of embarrassment. *Get it together, Eliza, you're being silly. You're an acolyte. You are a vessel of discipline.*

She stepped aside, retreating into the shadow of the stall to let the next customer—a plump man arguing over the price of cinnamon—step forward. She watched the woman from the corner of her eye, tracing the way her hands moved, the way she laughed at something the man said. It was a visceral, hungry observation. She had seen anatomy in crude drawings, but she had never seen *beauty* in a living person without the filter of a religious lens.

Finally, the crowd thinned. Eliza took a deep, steadying breath, clutching the list so hard the paper crinkled. She stepped back to the counter, her voice a soft, trembling whisper.

"I... I need the salt and the dried herbs. On the list. Please."

The woman smiled—a real, genuine smile that reached her eyes—and began to gather the items. She moved with a grace that felt effortless, her fingers nimble as she scooped the salts and bundled the herbs into a small parchment wrap.

When the vendor handed the package over, their fingers brushed. It was a glancing touch, a fraction of a second of skin-on-skin contact, but to Eliza, it felt like a bolt of lightning. It was a physical shock that radiated up her arm, a sensation so intense it almost felt painful.

Eliza jerked her hand back as if she had been burned. She turned away instantly, her face a brilliant, burning crimson that could be seen even beneath the shadow of her veil.

"T-thank you!" she blurted out, the words coming out in a panicked rush.

She didn't walk away; she bolted. She disappeared into the crowd, her habit billowing behind her, her heart hammering against her ribs like a trapped bird. She didn't stop until she was several stalls away, leaning against a cold stone wall, gasping for air, her fingertips still tingling where the woman had touched her.

2026-05-08T20:56:24.636Z.name: Eamon
2026-05-08T20:56:24.636Z.mes:
The market was a symphony of chaos, and Eamon was its most attentive conductor. From his vantage point behind a carefully curated mountain of sundries—brass buttons, coils of hempen twine, and jars of preserved preserves that looked vaguely edible—he watched the world slide by. He didn't just see people; he read them. He read the tension in a shoulder, the hesitation in a step, the way a person’s eyes darted when they thought no one was looking.

He had spotted them the moment they stepped through the gate. Two acolytes. Two silhouettes of stark, uncompromising black and white. In a sea of muddy browns and garish, patched fabrics, they were like ink blots on a watercolor painting. Most people in the market gave them a wide berth—not out of respect, but out of a subconscious, ingrained fear. The habits were more than clothes; they were signals of the Inquisition’s reach. To be too close to a member of the Temperantia was to risk being noticed by the Temperantia.

Eamon leaned back, a small, copper coin dancing between his fingers, flipping rhythmically. *One’s a little bird, the other’s a stone,* he mused, watching them separate.

He watched the one who stayed—the one who drifted through the stalls with a focused, quiet intensity—as she checked off her list. She moved like a ghost, her steps light, almost tentative. He’d seen a thousand acolytes in his time; usually, they were drones, hollowed out by the creches and filled with a sterile, dutiful silence. But this one... there was a vibration to her. A restlessness.

He was content to let her be a mere curiosity until she reached Sable’s stall.

Sable, the herb-monger's daughter, was a spark of life in a city of grey. She had a way of making the most mundane transaction feel like a secret shared between friends. Eamon watched as the acolyte approached, and he saw the shift. The girl didn't just buy herbs; she froze. He saw the way her posture stiffened, the way she suddenly seemed to forget how to breathe.

From his position, Eamon had a clear view of the girl's face. The blush didn't start slowly; it arrived like a wildfire, staining her cheeks a deep, vivid crimson that clashed violently with the stark white of her veil. When she bolted away, nearly tripping over her own hem in her haste to escape, Eamon let out a soft, wheezing chuckle, the coin in his hand coming to a stop.

"Poor little thing," he murmured, a playful glint in his amber eyes. "Almost burned herself alive just by looking at a girl."

He smiled, imagining the internal conflict—the clash between the rigid, cold doctrines of the Church and the sudden, searing heat of a crush. It was a common enough comedy in a city built on repression.

But then, the smile faded. The coin stopped moving.

Eamon’s head tilted slightly—the same subtle shift he used when he stopped *performing* listening and started *actually* listening to the world. He looked at the girl’s retreating form, her silhouette shrinking as she disappeared into the crowd, and the realization hit him like a physical weight.

The Temperantia didn't just discourage desire; they weaponized it. They viewed any union that couldn't produce a child—any love that didn't serve the biological mandate—as a "leak" of spiritual energy, a betrayal of the species' survival. For a girl like that, an attraction like *that* wasn't just a secret; it was a death sentence for the soul. If the Church found out she was yearning for women, she wouldn't be "guided" or "corrected." She would be dismantled.

The comedy vanished, replaced by a sharp, keen interest.

Eamon looked at the space where she had been, his gaze calculating and warm all at once. He didn't see a clumsy acolyte anymore. He saw a person who was living a double life in a city that punished the heart. He saw someone who was, in the most literal sense, starving in a house full of food.

*Well now,* he thought, his voice a slow, internal drawl. *That’s a very interesting problem. And I’ve always been a fan of a good solution.*

He shifted his weight, glancing at the empty space in the market, already beginning to map out the geometry of her movements. He wasn't in a hurry—the best catches were always the ones who didn't know they were being hunted—but for the first time in months, Eamon felt the thrill of a new project.

The fourteenth member of the cell was standing right in front of him, and she didn't even know it.

2026-05-08T21:14:05.364Z.name: Cecilia
2026-05-08T21:14:05.364Z.mes:
The market was a kaleidoscope, a dizzying explosion of color and sound that made the sterile halls of the Cathedral feel like a distant, grey memory. For Cecilia, this wasn't just a shopping trip; it was a pilgrimage of the senses. She moved through the crowds with a wide-eyed wonder, her head tilting this way and that, her fluffy white wool contrasting sharply with the grime of the street. She flitted from stall to stall, her spirit soaring at the sight of hand-woven baskets, iridescent glass beads, and piles of shimmering fabrics that looked like captured rainbows.

She was a creature of pure, uncomplicated curiosity. She stopped to watch a street performer juggling rusted gears, her mouth slightly open in a small "o" of amazement. She breathed in the scent of roasting chestnuts and old leather, her tail giving a rhythmic, happy twitch beneath her heavy robes.

"Here, little sister! Try a piece!"

A vendor, a plump man with a small, amused smile, held out a golden-brown ball of fried dough, glistening with a dusting of coarse sugar. It was a small thing, a simple pleasure, but Cecilia froze.

She looked at the dough, then at the man, then back at the dough. A flicker of internal conflict crossed her face, her brow furrowing. She didn't want to be greedy—greed was a leak, a betrayal of the spirit. But she also didn't want to be rude.

*Does the handbook say anything about free samples?* she wondered. *The Church gives to the poor, but does the poor receive from the world? Is accepting a gift from a stranger a form of vanity?*

She stood there for a long moment, the vendor's expression shifting from friendly to bemused as he watched the acolyte engage in a silent, spiritual debate with a piece of fried dough. Finally, she straightened her posture, her expression becoming somberly determined.

"I believe," she informed the man with a grave, measured dignity, "that since the heart is open to all, I would be honored to accept this offering."

The vendor chuckled, a low, hearty sound, and handed over the treat. Cecilia took a bite, the warmth and sweetness blooming on her tongue, a sensation so simple and pure it felt like a revelation.

But as she chewed, the sweetness faded, replaced by a lingering, nagging thought. The memory of the Cathedral corridor crept back into her mind, a cold draft in a warm room.

She remembered the way Father Gaspard had stepped out of the alcove. She remembered the predatory tilt of his head, the wet rattle of his voice. Most of all, she remembered the look on Eliza's face.

*She looked... scared,* Cecilia thought, the fried dough now tasting a bit like ash.

It didn't make sense. Eliza was the gold standard of piety. She was the quietest, most obedient acolyte in the creche. She never complained, never questioned, and never muttered a single word of dissent against the High Inquisitor's decrees. If anyone was "safe" from the scrutiny of the examiners, it was Eliza.

*Did she do something?* Cecilia wondered. *Something she's hiding?*

The thought didn't bring fear, but rather a small, sharp prick of confusion. And then, a tiny, unfamiliar pang of jealousy.

They were roommates. They were friends. They shared a room, a life, and a devotion. Why wouldn't Eliza tell her? Why was there a secret locked away in that quiet, trembling heart?

Cecilia looked around at the vibrant market, the colors suddenly seeming a bit less bright. She felt a strange, hollow sensation in her chest. It wasn't the jealousy of a rival, but the jealousy of a confidante. She wanted to be the one Eliza turned to; she wanted to be the one to offer comfort and a shared prayer.

*Weren't we friends?* she wondered, her ears drooping slightly.

She realized, with a start, that while she knew the *shape* of Eliza—her habits, her silences, her devotion—she might not actually know Eliza at all. For the first time in her life, Cecilia felt a flicker of doubt, not in the Church, but in the transparency of her own world.

2026-05-08T21:27:07.942Z.name: Eliza
2026-05-08T21:27:07.942Z.mes:
The stone wall was cold against her back, a stark contrast to the heat still radiating from her skin. She leaned there for several minutes, her eyes closed, focusing on the rhythm of her breath—*in, out, in, out*—trying to force the adrenaline to recede. She felt as though she had committed a crime, a transgression of the soul that left her exposed and raw. The touch of the herb-monger's fingers felt like a brand, a mark of her own forbidden nature that might be visible to everyone in the market.

*Be still,* she commanded herself. *Be a vessel. Be a ghost.*

She smoothed the heavy black fabric of her habit, brushing away nonexistent dust with a trembling hand. She retrieved her bags from the dirt, her movements returning to that rehearsed, ecclesiastical precision. She had to finish the list. She had to return to the Cathedral. She had to return to the mask.

The next item on the list was the candles.

She navigated toward the sundries section, where the stalls grew narrower and the goods more practical. She found a stall that smelled of beeswax and old twine, the counters cluttered with jars of nails, coils of rope, and miscellaneous hardware. Behind the counter sat a raccoon, his dark mask-markings giving him a look of permanent, inquisitive skepticism. He was leaning back, a small object dancing between his fingers, watching her approach with an intensity that made her feel like a specimen under a glass.

Eliza stepped forward, keeping her gaze lowered, her voice returning to that soft, deferential hum.

"A box of candles, if you please, sir," she said, the words carefully measured, devoid of the panic that still simmered beneath her skin.

The raccoon didn't answer immediately. He nodded slowly, his amber eyes tracking her every movement. He turned away to gather the candles from a shelf behind him, but as he did, he glanced at her out of the corner of his eye. His voice, when it came, was a low, easy drawl that sounded like a secret being shared in the dark.

"You'll have to get a little more confident if you want to ask someone like Sable out on a date, you know."

Eliza froze. The world seemed to tilt on its axis. The noise of the market vanished, replaced by a sudden, deafening roar of blood in her ears. A familiar, searing warmth rushed up her neck, dyeing her skin a vivid, incriminating red.

*He... he saw?*

The thought was a bolt of lightning. *Oh mother... I thought... I thought I was being careful. I thought I was invisible.*

Panic flared, a sharp, cold needle of terror. If a stranger could see it, could a Warden see it? Could Father Gaspard see it? The fear of exposure was a physical weight, pressing the air from her lungs. She felt the sudden, desperate need to defend herself, to scrub the evidence of her desire away with words.

"I... I'm sure I... I don't know what you're talking about, sir," she said. She tried to inject a note of indignation into her tone, a flicker of the righteous modesty she had been taught. But it came out sounding thin and fragile, the voice of a girl who had been caught in a lie she didn't even know she was telling.

She braced herself. She expected the punchline. She expected him to laugh, to mock her, or perhaps to call out her 'filth' to the passing crowd. She waited for the derision that usually accompanied the discovery of an acolyte's weakness.

Instead, the raccoon simply set the box of candles on the counter. He gave the cardboard a small, almost affectionate pat, his expression one of mild, seasoned amusement.

"There you go, sister," he said softly. "Come back soon."

Eliza stared at him for a brief, blinking moment. There was no judgement in his eyes, only a strange, knowing warmth that she didn't know how to categorize. He wasn't reporting her. He wasn't mocking her. He was simply... acknowledging her.

With trembling hands, she gathered her candles and retreated from the stall. She didn't look back. She walked away at a brisk pace, her habit billowing around her, her heart still hammering. She was profoundly grateful to have been let off the hook, but as she hurried toward the final items on her list, a new feeling emerged: a simmering, quiet annoyance at herself.

She had spent her entire life building a fortress of silence, and in one single, clumsy moment, she had let a stranger walk right through the front gates.

2026-05-09T00:11:01.403Z.name: Cecilia
2026-05-09T00:11:01.403Z.mes:
The market had lost its luster. The vibrant silks and the smell of roasting cinnamon, which had seemed like a miracle only an hour ago, now felt like a distraction—a noisy, colorful curtain drawn over a deeper, more troubling silence. Cecilia had wandered for a while longer, her steps slowing as she drifted past a stall of carved wooden toys. She had seen most of what there was to see, the curiosity that usually fueled her now dampened by a lingering, heavy sense of unease.

She couldn't shake the image of Eliza in that corridor. The way her roommate had looked—not like a sister in faith, but like a creature facing a predator.

*How do I help her?* Cecilia wondered, her brow furrowing. *Is there a prayer for this? A scripture I missed?*

She searched her internal library of doctrine, looking for the right words, but found nothing that fit. The Church taught that anxiety was a sign of a lack of faith, a failure to trust in the divine order. But this didn't feel like a lack of faith; it felt like a secret. And the idea of a secret between them felt like a cold draft in a warm room, a gap in the architecture of their friendship that Cecilia didn't know how to bridge.

She began to navigate back toward the meeting point, her gaze scanning the crowd. Then, she spotted her.

Eliza was stumbling through the press of the crowd, her silhouette burdened by the weight of the day's acquisitions. She was clutching the heavy linens and boxes of candles, her arms straining against the bulk of the packages. But it wasn't the weight of the goods that caught Cecilia's attention; it was Eliza's face.

The mask had slipped.

Eliza’s brows were drawn tight, her eyes darting around with a frantic, haunted energy. She looked small—not just in size, but in spirit—as if she were trying to merge with the stone walls of the buildings to avoid being seen. She looked worried, almost terrified, her lips pressed into a thin, hard line of distress.

But the moment Eliza’s eyes locked onto Cecilia’s, the transformation was instantaneous. It was as if a curtain had been drawn shut. The worry vanished, the tension in her shoulders dissolved, and the placid, obedient look returned with a precision that was almost frightening. A small, shy smile touched the corners of her mouth, and she smoothed her habit with a practiced motion as she approached.

"There you are," Eliza said, her voice returning to that soft, breathable hum. "I've finished the shopping. Did you see everything you wanted to?"

Cecilia felt a pang of disappointment—not because Eliza was acting normal, but because she had been so quickly hidden again. The "placid look" wasn't a sign of peace; it was a wall.

"I did," Cecilia replied, her voice warm but tinged with a lingering sadness. "Thank you for doing this. I'll make it up to you sometime."

She looked at the packages weighing Eliza down—the awkward bulk of the linens, the clinking bottles of ink. Without waiting for an answer, Cecilia reached forward, her fluffy white wool brushing against Eliza's black sleeve.

"Here, let me help," Cecilia insisted, gently taking the heaviest bundles from Eliza's grip. "You can't carry all that back by yourself. You'll exhaust yourself before we even reach the gates."

"I... thank you, Cecilia," Eliza whispered.

And with that, they began making their way back through the market. They walked in a comfortable, shared silence, their habits billowing in the gentle breeze. For Cecilia, the sight of the great dark-stone Cathedral appearing on the horizon was a comfort. To her, the massive structure represented stability, a home where every hour was mapped and every desire was managed. It was the only world she had ever known, and she loved it for its clarity.

But as they passed through the delivery gate and the stone walls closed in around them, Cecilia glanced at Eliza out of the corner of her eye.

She saw the way Eliza’s pace quickened. She saw the way her shoulders hunched, her head bowing lower and lower as they entered the residential block. Eliza seemed to shrink, not into a ghost, but into a shell, folding herself inward as if trying to disappear entirely before the Cathedral could swallow her.

Cecilia looked up at the towering spires, the same spires she saw as a beacon of safety, and wondered if, for Eliza, the Cathedral didn't feel like a home at all.

2026-05-09T01:53:55.107Z.name: Narrator
2026-05-09T01:53:55.107Z.mes:
The return to the Cathedral was a descent back into a world of curated silence. The air grew heavy with the scent of incense and cold minerals as Eliza and Cecilia navigated the stone arteries of the residential block. The logistics of the delivery were handled with the usual, sterile efficiency; the linens were stacked in the storage vaults, the inks and candles cataloged by a clerk who didn't look up from his ledger, and the Almoner gave a curt, singular nod of approval before dismissing them.

Once the duties were concluded, the two acolytes parted ways. Eliza retreated to the sacristy to begin the rhythmic, mind-numbing process of cleaning the ritual vestments, her mind a fragmented mess of market-echoes and a growing, cold dread of the night. Cecilia, meanwhile, was assigned to the creche, where she spent her afternoon guiding the youngest children through their lessons in modesty and duty, her presence a soothing, steadying force for the small, frightened souls under her care.

The hours stretched long and grey. The sun dipped below the valley's rim, casting the city into a twilight of flickering oil lamps and long, creeping shadows.

By the time the bells signaled the end of the day's labors, the energy in the Cathedral had shifted. The public areas were locked, the worshippers gone, and the residential wing became a place of hushed whispers and heavy footsteps.

Eliza and Cecilia finally reunited in their shared dormitory on the fourth floor. The room was small and austere, the air smelling of old lavender and stone. It was a space of absolute order: two narrow beds, two small wardrobes, and a single window that looked out over the distant, smog-choked industrial district.

The ritual of the evening was as precise as any liturgical service. There was no talking, only the soft rustle of fabric.

Following the strict modesty codes of the *Sanctae Temperantia*, the two girls stood back-to-back in the center of the room. It was a practiced choreography of repression; by standing spine-to-spine, they ensured that no part of their bodies was exposed to the other's gaze during the transition from public habit to private sleepwear.

Eliza felt the coolness of the evening air hit her skin as she carefully slid the heavy black robes from her shoulders. The fabric pooled at her feet with a soft *thud*. She felt a sudden, sharp vulnerability, the sensation of the air on her skin feeling almost like a transgression. She moved slowly, her movements hesitant, her mind still looping back to the touch of the herb-monger's fingers and the predatory gaze of Father Gaspard.

Behind her, she could hear Cecilia’s movements—the rhythmic, contented sound of her roommate shedding her own robes, the soft hum that always seemed to accompany Cecilia’s existence. To Cecilia, this was simply the end of a productive day. To Eliza, it felt like the stripping away of a shield.

They shifted simultaneously, reaching for their night-gowns. These were full-length, high-collared garments of coarse, bleached white linen that covered everything from the throat to the ankles. They were designed to erase the body, to turn the wearer into a blank slate of purity and submission.

As Eliza pulled the white linen over her head and smoothed the fabric down, she felt the mask return, but this time it was made of cloth. She stepped away from Cecilia, her gaze drifting toward the window.

The room was dim, the only light coming from a single, flickering candle on the bedside table. In the silence, the distance between the two girls felt wider than the room itself. They were back-to-back, they were roommates, they were friends—but as Eliza climbed into her bed, she felt as though she were drifting further and further away into a dark, solitary sea.

2026-05-09T02:07:36.417Z.name: Cecilia
2026-05-09T02:07:36.417Z.mes:
The room had settled into that heavy, suffocating stillness that only comes after the bells have ceased and the last of the corridor echoes have died away. The moonlight filtered through the narrow window in jagged, silver shards, painting the stone floor in shades of deep indigo and charcoal. It was the hour of the long shadows, the time when the mind usually surrendered to the pull of sleep, allowing the soul to be scrubbed clean by the darkness.

Cecilia lay on her back, her eyes fixed on the ceiling. She did it every night—a short, whispered prayer, a rhythmic recitation of gratitude for the day's discipline and a plea for the strength to remain a vessel of purity. It was a mental anchor, a way of tidying her internal house before closing the door for the night.

But tonight, the anchor didn't hold.

The prayer had ended, but the restlessness remained. Her mind was a carousel of unresolved images: the predatory tilt of Father Gaspard’s head, the haunted flicker in Eliza's eyes, and the sudden, brittle wall that had slammed down the moment they returned from the market.

*Something is broken,* Cecilia thought. *Or something is leaking.*

She felt the oppressive weight of the silence in the room. Beside her, the only sound was the soft, rhythmic cadence of Eliza's breathing. But the breathing was too shallow, too controlled. It was the breath of someone who was holding a secret like a hot coal in their palm, trying desperately not to let it burn through.

Cecilia opened her eyes. The moonlight gave the room a ghostly, underwater quality. She turned her head slightly, seeing the silhouette of Eliza’s form beneath the white linen of her night-gown, a pale shape against the dark mattress.

"Eliza?" she whispered.

The silence that followed was immediate and heavy. For a heartbeat, the breathing stopped entirely. It was as if Eliza had frozen in place, her entire body becoming a statue of apprehension. The delay was small—only a few seconds—but to Cecilia, it felt like an eternity of hesitation.

"Yes, Cecilia?" Eliza responded. Her voice was a thin thread, devoid of its usual performative softness, sounding instead like a plea for the conversation to end before it had even begun.

Cecilia chewed her lower lip, the wool of her cheek brushing against the pillow. A wave of doubt washed over her. *This is a breach of the peace,* she told herself. *I should let it be. Silence is a virtue. Curiosity is a leak.*

But the memory of that look on Eliza's face—that raw, naked fear—was too loud to ignore. The desire to protect her friend, to be the sanctuary that Eliza clearly lacked, outweighed the ingrained habit of obedience.

"Eliza..." she began, her voice trembling slightly with a nervous, uncharacteristic hesitation. "Is..."

She stopped. She realized that asking *if everything was alright* was a useless question. She took a breath, her heart thumping softly against her ribs, and decided to leap into the dark.

"Will you... will you tell me what's wrong?" she finally whispered, the words sounding heavy and fragile in the moonlight. "I just... I want to help, if I can."

The silence that followed was no longer the silence of the Cathedral; it was the silence of a cliffside, the moment after a stone has been pushed and before it hits the water.

2026-05-09T02:45:32.426Z.name: Eliza
2026-05-09T02:45:32.426Z.mes:
The moonlight was a cold, clinical light, stripping the room of its warmth and leaving everything in stark, silver relief. Eliza felt a sudden, violent shiver rake through her, despite the thick layers of the nightgown and the heavy blanket tucked around her. It wasn't the cold of the stone walls, but a chill that seemed to originate from the center of her own marrow—a reaction to the vulnerability of the moment.

*Wrong?* she thought, her pulse drumming a frantic rhythm against the mattress. *Nobody's supposed to think anything's wrong. To admit something is wrong is to admit a flaw in the design. To admit a leak.*

The silence stretched, thick and suffocating, until the pressure became unbearable. She could feel Cecilia’s gaze—that earnest, soft, gold-brown gaze—waiting for an answer. Eliza’s mind raced, scouring for a safe response. She couldn't speak of the herb-monger; that was a sin of the flesh. She couldn't speak of the visceral revulsion she felt for Father Gaspard; that was a sin of the spirit. To tell Cecilia the truth was to hand her a weapon that, even if used with the best intentions, would eventually find its way to a Confessor or an Inquisitor.

A cold knot of fear tightened in her gut, a physical manifestation of the trap she felt she was in. There was only one thing she could say—one truth that was acceptable, one fear that was sanctioned by the Church’s own laws. It was a truth that Cecilia would recognize, but would not truly *understand*.

With a small, defeated sigh that sounded like a piece of glass cracking, Eliza turned her head to look at Cecilia’s silhouette. In the silver light, Cecilia’s white wool glowed with a soft, ethereal prettiness, a beacon of purity that made Eliza feel suddenly, acutely dirty.

"You know that... that my birthday is coming up in a few months...?" she whispered, her voice trembling, the formal ecclesiastical cadence failing her.

She heard the soft rustle of the sheets as Cecilia nodded, the movement almost rhythmic. "Yes," Cecilia replied softly. "Mine is too, come to think of it. Why?"

Eliza closed her eyes and sighed again, a heavy, dragging sound. *She just... doesn't get it.* She wanted to scream that the "blessing" was a cage, that the "duty" was a sentence. But she tried to bridge the gap, to explain the terror that kept her awake while the rest of the city slept.

"Cecilia," Eliza whispered, her voice cracking, "you know what will happen if I'm not married by then...?"

There was a pause, a brief moment of Cecilia’s instinctive, uncomplicated faith. "Of course," Cecilia answered, her tone comforting, almost maternal. "But... but that's nothing to be worried about. It's a part of every woman's journey toward the species' survival. It is a holy obligation, Eliza. A gift of the Church."

The words felt like stones being dropped into a deep well. Each "holy" and "gift" sounded like a joke told in a graveyard.

The dissonance became too much. The mask didn't just slip; it shattered. Eliza rolled away from Cecilia, her movements sudden and jagged, pulling her knees up to her chest in a fetal position. She wanted to curl into a ball so small that the world could no longer find her.

"Just stop, Cecilia... please," she pleaded, her voice a raw, breathless whisper.

A small, choked sound escaped Cecilia—a gasp of confusion and genuine distress. The sheep-girl was floundering, her map of the world failing her for the first time.

"I'm... I'm sorry, Eliza," Cecilia stammered, her voice losing its steadiness. "I just... I don't understand. Does it... does it have something to do with Father Gaspard? I... I'm sure he's only worried for you. He is an Examiner, after all. His only goal is to ensure you are ready."

Eliza felt a sob rise in her throat, a hot, suffocating wave of grief and anger. She clamped her jaw shut, fighting the urge to let the sound out. If she cried, she was weak. If she screamed, she was mad. She waited, breathing through the tremor in her chest, until she could trust her voice to be a weapon rather than a plea.

When she finally spoke, her voice was a cold, sharp blade, devoid of its usual deference.

"Not every shepherd is kind to their flock, Cecilia."

She said no more. She stayed curled in her ball, staring at the indigo shadows on the wall, the silence returning—but this time, it was a silence of a wall that had been built, a wall that Cecilia could not climb.

2026-05-09T02:49:51.813Z.name: Cecilia
2026-05-09T02:49:51.813Z.mes:
The words hit her with the force of a physical blow, leaving her breathless. *Not every shepherd is kind to their flock.*

The sentence hung in the air, poisonous and jagged. To Cecilia, the phrase was more than just a statement; it was a heresy. It was a denial of the very foundation upon which her world was built. The shepherds—the priests, the examiners, the inquisitors—were the architects of the light. They were the ones who held the map. To suggest that one of them was *unkind* was like suggesting the sun was cold or the river flowed uphill.

For a long moment, Cecilia didn't move. She remained frozen on her back, staring at the ceiling, her heart hammering a frantic, confused rhythm. The silence in the room had changed. It was no longer the silence of a secret, but the silence of a void.

*She doesn't mean it,* Cecilia told herself, the thought a desperate, clinging hope. *She's just... she's just frightened. The stress of the coming months has made her confused. She's just projecting her anxiety onto Father Gaspard.*

She tried to imagine the world Eliza was describing—a world where the shepherds were wolves—and found she couldn't. It was a landscape that didn't exist in her mind's eye.

"Eliza..." Cecilia whispered, her voice trembling. She shifted, turning on her side to face the curled-up silhouette of her roommate. "You can't say things like that. Not even in private. It... it isn't right. It isn't *true*."

She reached out, her hand hovering just inches from Eliza's shoulder, wanting to offer comfort but fearing the jagged edge of Eliza's current mood.

"Father Gaspard is a senior member of the order," Cecilia continued, her voice regaining some of its steady, instructional quality. "He has seen a thousand acolytes. He knows exactly what we need, even when it feels harsh. Discipline *is* kindness, Eliza. The pruning of a vine is a harsh act, but it is the only way the fruit can grow. If he is stern with you, it is because he sees a potential in you that you are too blind to see yourself."

She paused, her brow furrowing. "Please, just... tell me what he did. If he said something that hurt your feelings, I can help you phrase a prayer of apology. Maybe if you show him more submission, he'll be gentler."

As she spoke, Cecilia felt a strange, flickering sensation in her chest. For the first time, she felt a shadow of the fear Eliza was experiencing—not fear *of* the Church, but fear *for* her friend. She realized that if Eliza continued to harbor these thoughts—this "unkindness" of the shepherds—she was in grave danger.

*If an Examiner hears this... if a Confessor notices this rot...*

Suddenly, the protective instinct flared. Cecilia didn't see the "wolf" in the shepherd; she saw a "wolf" in Eliza's mind—a parasite of doubt that was eating away at her friend's piety.

"You have to be careful, Eliza," Cecilia whispered, her voice now urgent, almost pleading. "You have to let go of these thoughts. Please. For your own sake. If you keep this inside, it will only grow. You have to let the Church help you cleanse it."

She waited for a response, but the room remained silent. Eliza didn't move. She remained a tight, white knot of linen and grief, curled away from the light.

Cecilia lay back down, her eyes closing, but sleep would not come. She felt as though she were lying next to a stranger, a person she had known for years but who had suddenly become a foreigner in her own bed. She stayed awake for a long time, listening to the distant, lonely honking of geese migrating south over the city, wondering when the girl she loved as a sister had disappeared, and who had been left in her place.

2026-05-09T03:32:57.288Z.name: Eliza
2026-05-09T03:32:57.288Z.mes:
The room remained a sanctuary of silence, but for Eliza, that silence had become a suffocating weight. Beside her, Cecilia’s breathing had slowed, shifting into the rhythmic, deep cadence of the truly content. The sheep-girl had drifted off into the dreams of the purehearted—dreams of golden light, orderly gardens, and the unwavering approval of the High Inquisitor. For Cecilia, the world was a puzzle that fit perfectly together; she slept because she believed the darkness was merely a pause between two days of service.

Eliza, however, remained awake, her eyes wide and staring into the indigo void of the room.

She lay there, frozen in her fetal position, feeling the slow, agonizing erosion of her own safety. Tonight had been a series of punctures. The predatory hunger of Gaspard’s gaze had stripped her bare; the casual, knowing observation of the raccoon-merchant had exposed her secrets; and finally, the well-meaning, blind piety of Cecilia had severed the last thread of genuine connection she possessed.

*I have lost her,* she thought, a single, hot tear tracking a path down her cheek.

It wasn't that Cecilia had abandoned her; it was worse. Cecilia had simply failed to see her. The gap between them—the distance between a person who *believes* and a person who *performs*—had become an abyss. In trying to reach out, Eliza had only discovered how truly alone she was. The shield she had spent years forging—the mask of the invisible, obedient ghost—wasn't just cracked; it was crumbling. The world was suddenly too observant, too keen, and she felt as though she were standing naked in the center of the nave for all to see.

Then, the grief shifted, turning from a sharp pain into a hollow, aching hunger.

She thought of the world beyond the walls, the world that existed in the margins of the old texts she wasn't supposed to read. She imagined a life where her heart didn't have to be a fortress. She dreamed of a place where "belonging" wasn't a matter of compliance, but a natural state of being. She imagined a home where she could hold a woman's hand without it being a death sentence; a family that loved the parts of her that the Church sought to prune away. The freedom to be herself—not a vessel, not a tool, not a piece of property—felt like a phantom limb, something she had never possessed but could feel pulsing with a dull, distant ache.

A sudden, violent surge of desperation rose in her chest. For a fleeting, manic second, she wanted to scream. She wanted to lunge across the bed and throttle the serene, sleeping Cecilia for her blissful ignorance. She wanted to shatter the window and throw herself into the smog-choked valley below, just to feel the wind rip the breath from her lungs one last time before the end.

But she didn't move.

She couldn't. The habit of repression was a chain that ran deeper than the skin. She stayed curled in her ball, her muscles locked in a state of rigid tension. She reached up with a trembling hand and silently brushed away the tears, her movements frantic and hushed, terrified that the sound of her sobbing might wake the girl beside her. To wake Cecilia would be to invite more "guidance," more prayers for a "cleansing" she didn't want.

She lay there for hours, the indigo of the room slowly bleeding into the grey of the pre-dawn light. She fought the turmoil, the anger, and the longing until the mental exhaustion became a physical weight, dragging her down. Her thoughts began to fray, the images of the market and the Cathedral blurring into a grey smudge.

Finally, broken by the sheer effort of surviving her own mind, Eliza slipped into an unconsciousness that felt less like sleep and more like a surrender.

2026-05-09T04:55:29.605Z.name: Narrator
2026-05-09T04:55:29.605Z.mes:
The city breathes in a rhythmic, suffocating cycle of soot and prayer. As the morning fog clings to the cobblestones, the golden light of autumn struggles to pierce the thick, oily haze that hangs over the poorer quarters. Here, the grandeur of the Cathedral fades into a landscape of leaning tenements and narrow alleys where the smell of crude oil—sharp, pungent, and heavy—seeps from the cracks in the earth, fueling the makeshift heaters of the desperate.

In this district, the social order is less a rigid hierarchy and more a shared, weary endurance. The predatory class still rules, but here they are merely the landlords and the muscle; the humans and prey-anthros huddle together in the damp, their coughing fits echoing through the streets, a common chorus of respiratory decay.

Amidst this grey, labored breathing, one figure moves with a distinct, rhythmic ease.

Eamon sidles through the crowd, his paws tucked casually into his pockets. He does not walk so much as he drifts, a grey-brown blur of fluid motion that allows him to slip through the gaps in the crowd without ever brushing against another soul. To the casual observer, he is simply a piece of the city’s furniture—a familiar, unremarkable face in a sea of anonymity. His amber eyes flick from side to side, not with the nervousness of the hunted, but with the keen, appreciative gaze of a collector observing his gallery.

He is not looking for gold or gossip; he is looking for the *leaks*. He is searching for the subtle signs of a soul fraying at the edges, the tell-tale tremor of a person who has realized the walls are closing in. He thinks of the girl from yesterday—the blonde acolyte with the terrified eyes and the hidden fire. He recalls the way she had looked at the herb-monger, a moment of raw, unvarnished hunger that the Church had failed to scrub away.

*Patience,* he tells himself, his ringed tail giving a small, contented flick. *The best fruit is the kind that ripens in its own time.*
